the textarea is sticking it slightly too far to the right. it's causing a horizontal scroll on mobile. can you carefully diagnose that?
Codebuff

Okay, a horizontal scrollbar on mobile usually means an element is wider than the viewport, often due to padding, borders, or margins not being accounted for correctly with width: 100%, or an element having a fixed width that's too large.

Let's look at the styles for the textarea and its container in src/Reciplier.module.css and how they are applied in src/Reciplier.js.

You've hit on a very common CSS issue! When an element has width: 100% and also has horizontal padding or borders, its total width can exceed 100% of its parent container, causing overflow and that pesky horizontal scrollbar.

In your src/Reciplier.module.css, the textarea (and other input elements) are styled with width: 100%, and the textarea also gets padding: 0.75rem (from the .p-3 class) and a 1px border.

The fix is to use the box-sizing: border-box; CSS property. This tells the browser to include the padding and border in the element's total width and height, rather than adding them on top.

I'll add this to the general rule for input elements in your src/Reciplier.module.css.

This change should ensure that the textarea, even with its padding and border, correctly fits within its container without causing overflow.

Please save the change, restart your development server, and check if the horizontal scrollbar issue on mobile is resolved.

The gh-pages tool keeps a local cache. Deleting it can force it to re-evaluate the files to be deployed.

Based on my careful reading of both files, here's a comprehensive checklist for faithfully implementing the spec in the README:

---

Implementation Checklist for Generalized Reciplier

Parsing & Syntax

  • [ ] Parse curly-brace expressions {...} from template text
  • [ ] Support labeled expressions with format {label: expression} (e.g., {d:9}, {r: d/2})
  • [ ] Support unlabeled expressions like {1x}, {3x} — auto-generate nonce labels (e.g., {var01: 1x})
  • [ ] Support bare labels with no initial value like {w:} — solver must find a valid value
  • [ ] Support multiple equations per expression separated by = (e.g., {A: 1/2*tau*r^2 = w*h})
  • [ ] Support pure constraints without labels (e.g., {a^2 + b^2 = c^2})
  • [ ] Support Mathematica-style implicit multiplication where 2x means 2*x, 0.621371vb means 0.621371*vb
  • [ ] Support scaling factor x — expressions like {12x} mean 12 * x
  • [ ] Preserve arbitrary markdown/HTML in templates (including HTML comments for hidden constraints)
  • [ ] Error on duplicate labels — same label for two expressions is an error
  • [ ] Allow multiple references to the same variable

Solver / Constraint System

  • [ ] Search for variable assignments that satisfy all equations simultaneously
  • [ ] Favor positive, finite numbers when multiple solutions exist
  • [ ] Handle impossible templates gracefully — change variables arbitrarily (no clever heuristics; Anti-Magic)
  • [ ] Binary search approach for finding valid assignments (current method)
  • [ ] Handle redundant constraints gracefully (e.g., {d = 2r} when r is already defined as d/2)

UI Behavior

  • [ ] Render each expression as a numeric input field
  • [ ] Insta-update all fields when any field changes
  • [ ] Support marking fields as "fixed" — slick UI to toggle this
  • [ ] Fixed fields don't auto-recompute when other fields change
  • [ ] Show violated equations in red for non-fixed fields when constraints can't be satisfied
  • [ ] Display violated equations as "25 != 36" style (actual != expected)
  • [ ] Recompute on blur — when clicking away from a field, recompute its value to satisfy constraints
  • [ ] Block fixing fields in violated state — can't mark a field as fixed when equations are violated

Dropdown / Recipes

  • [ ] Support dropdown of predefined recipes (like "Breakaway Biscuits")
  • [ ] Include example recipes:
  • Pan-scaling recipe (the main example)
  • Pythagorean triple example
  • Breakaway Biscuits (bike race gap calculator)
  • Family bike tour timing calculator

Development Principles (from AGENTS.md)

  • [ ] Anti-Magic Principle — don't add if-statements to fix edge cases; fail explicitly
  • [ ] Anti-Robustness/Anti-Postel — fail loudly and immediately; never silently fix inputs
  • [ ] Pareto Dominance — any change must be a Pareto improvement or get explicit approval
  • [ ] Preserve human-written comments exactly — don't even change whitespace
  • [ ] Don't delete human-written code — comment out instead with explanation
  • [ ] Call tests "quals" not tests

Future/Deferred (noted in spec but not immediate)

  • [ ] Consider more sophisticated solving (e.g., Mathematica's NMinimize) for cases requiring multi-variable simultaneous changes
  • [ ] Alternate ERB-style syntax (<% %>, <%= %>, <%# %>) — noted as "for later"

---

This checklist covers all the explicit and implicit requirements from the README spec while respecting the development principles in AGENTS.md. Should I proceed with implementing any of these items?

You're right, let's discuss the design. The current behavior is:

  1. HTML comments like <!-- {s: h+m/60} --> are being rendered as visible text (escaped) in the output
  2. The {...} blocks inside comments ARE being parsed and their expressions ARE being processed (which is correct - they define hidden variables/constraints)

The question is: what SHOULD happen with HTML comments?

Looking at the README spec:

"you can, for example, put intermediate equations you don't want cluttering the recipe in html comments"

So the intent is:

  • Parse the {...} blocks inside comments (for variable definitions and constraints) ✓
  • Don't display the comments at all in the rendered output ✗ (currently broken)

Design options:

  1. Strip HTML comments entirely from rendered output - The simplest approach. Comments exist only to define hidden variables/constraints. They never appear in the UI.
  1. Render comments as actual HTML comments - So they'd be in the DOM but invisible. This seems pointless for a recipe app.
  1. Show comments in a collapsible "debug" section - For power users who want to see the constraints.

I think option 1 is the right approach - just don't render the comment text at all. The {...} blocks inside are still parsed and processed, but when rendering, we skip over the comment ranges entirely.

07:05
i don't understand your argument that first-wins is safer
Copilot Chat copilot/gpt-5.2 thought for 23s

“Safer” here is about minimizing the blast radius of an error, not about mathematical correctness.

Given “duplicate label” is already an error, we’re forced to pick *some* behavior for the rest of the pipeline (render fields, evaluate constraints, etc.). There are three plausible choices:

  1. first-wins (current, via continue)
  2. last-wins (stomp)
  3. “don’t pick” (treat it as unusable/undefined)

(3) would be the purest “fail loudly”, but it would ripple through a lot of code paths (tons of knock-on undefined-variable errors, missing fields, etc.) and it’s the biggest behavior change.

Between (1) and (2), first-wins is “safer” in the sense that it makes accidental duplicates *less able to silently change the meaning of everything that came before*:

  • Example: earlier you have {x:1} and later you accidentally type another {x:2}.
  • With last-wins, suddenly *all* computed numbers that depend on x jump to “2x” even though the user’s original definition is still sitting there in the text. The banner is showing, but the page’s numbers are now globally different, which is exactly the kind of “surprising magic” you generally don’t want while in an error state.
  • With first-wins, the original behavior stays intact and the duplicate is flagged as an error. The mistake is localized to “this later cell is wrong” instead of rewriting the semantics of the whole doc.

Also, stomping makes behavior depend on incidental ordering: if someone moves the duplicate earlier/later in the text, the “winner” changes, which changes computed values even though the error is “the same”.

So “first-wins is safer” = “in the presence of an error, keep the rest of the document behaving as close as possible to what it was before the mistake was introduced”, rather than letting the later mistake override earlier intent.

If you want the “least if-statement-y” semantics to be last-wins anyway, that’s totally consistent too — it’s just a different tradeoff: simpler loop, but bigger semantic swing during error states.

Copilot Chat copilot/gpt-5.2 thought for 34s

They’re equivalent only in an idealized solver. In practice (especially with a heuristic/greedy solver like we currently have), they diverge in two important ways.

Two meanings

  1. Frozen = semantic constraint (“hard equation”)

Freezing a cell means: “the value of this variable must equal its current number.”
Formally you add a constraint like $v = 12$ (or, in your spec language, append the literal 12 to that cell’s elist).

  1. Frozen = algorithmic restriction (“don’t touch this knob”)

Freezing a cell means: “the solver is not allowed to adjust this variable while trying to satisfy constraints.”
Formally: you don’t add any new equation; you just exclude that variable from the set of variables the solver may change.

How they differ when things are overconstrained

In a perfect solver, (2) is basically an implementation technique for (1). But in a *non-perfect* solver, (2) can fail for reasons that are not true “unsat”, and it can also fail to *explain* failure.

Concrete differences:

  • Unsat vs solver-stuck:

With (1), “frozen” participates in the *constraint system*, so if you can’t satisfy everything you can honestly say “overconstrained (unsat)”.
With (2), you might fail simply because your search strategy can’t find the solution given the restricted knobs — even if a solution exists that respects the intended freeze semantics. In that case “overconstrained” would be a false positive; the truth is “solver couldn’t find a solution”.

  • Blame / diagnosis:

With (1), the solver can attribute unsat to the frozen-equality constraints you injected (“these freezes + these equations conflict”).
With (2), there is no explicit “freeze constraint” in the system, so you can’t distinguish “unsat due to freezes” from “heuristic didn’t make progress”.

  • Frozen derived fields (subtle but important):

Suppose a cell is definition-like, e.g. a: 3x. If the user “freezes the *field a*”, the semantic meaning (1) is: add a = 30 (if it currently displays 30). That indirectly constrains x (since a=3x).
If you interpret freezing as (2) and only say “don’t adjust a”, but a is normally recomputed from x, then “freezing” doesn’t actually constrain x unless you also inject the equality. You end up with “a is frozen” as a UI promise, but the math system doesn’t get the corresponding constraint unless you use (1).

So when you’re overconstrained, (1) gives you a principled definition: the constraint set has no solution. (2) gives you: the solver didn’t find a solution while forbidden from touching certain variables — which might be true unsat, or might be solver weakness.

If you tell me which “freeze” you want in the spec for derived cells like a:3x (freeze the displayed value of a, or freeze the underlying variables like x), I can map that cleanly to a single semantics and avoid magic.

I’m going to read and compare it to the current solvem() in , then I’ll give a concrete review focused on semantics (frozen/constraints), failure modes, and qual impact.It’s an interesting hybrid solver (symbolic-ish propagation + a gradient-descent cleanup), but as-written I wouldn’t drop it in as Reciplier’s solvem() without tightening a few semantics and failure modes.

What’s good

  • The “logic & algebra pass” does useful propagation when there’s a clear anchor (literal number or evaluable term), and the “dependency enforcement” idea (treating a = f(x) as an always-enforced definition) matches the way recipes want derived cells to behave.
  • It treats constant expressions (no variable deps) as “hard” anchors (h = 3), which aligns with the spec direction that 628/100 and 6.28 should behave like “bare numbers”.

Main problems (relative to Reciplier’s current spec + engineering rules)

  • Variable universe is taken from initialVars keys only. varNames = Object.keys(initialVars) means any variable that appears in an equation but isn’t present in initialVars won’t be a parameter to new Function(...). In practice that can yield runtime ReferenceError (not caught) or silently wrong behavior, depending on the expression. Reciplier’s current solver can introduce new vars as it solves; this one basically can’t unless everything is predeclared.
  • Runtime evaluation errors aren’t contained. The compile step catches new Function construction errors, but a runtime error inside the generated function (eg ReferenceError from a missing var) will throw during f(...values) and crash the solve, rather than failing loudly in a controlled way or producing a clean “unsat” signal.
  • It silently “makes up” values. Unknowns go null/undefined → NaN → 0.5 (PRE-OPTIMIZATION). That’s very “Postel”; it can hide modeling mistakes and makes it harder to reason about “no solution” vs “not enough constraints”.
  • Internal “pinning” goes beyond explicit frozen-ness. Anything with anchorH === 3 causes variables to become pinned, and anchorH can become 3 not only from literal numbers / constant expressions, but also from expressions whose deps currently have strength 3. That can effectively freeze things that are merely *derived* from frozen values, which is not the same as “cell is frozen because its ceqn contains a bare number”.
  • No explicit notion of “unsat” / residual. It always returns a numeric assignment. That’s not necessarily a deal-breaker (Reciplier already uses post-checking via eqnsSatisfied), but combined with the silent defaulting and pinning, it can return something that looks “reasonable” while being quite far from satisfying constraints.

If you want to keep this approach, the minimum changes I’d require

  • Build varNames from the equations (parse identifiers) ∪ initialVars, not just initialVars.
  • Wrap *every* equation evaluation in try/catch and treat exceptions as non-finite, so the solver can keep going and the UI can show the “no solution / overconstrained” banner via post-checking.
  • Remove the NaN → 0.5 fill (or at least gate it behind an explicit “we are optimizing” phase that only runs when you already have a fully-declared variable set and you’ve decided that’s acceptable).
  • Restrict pinned to things that are explicitly frozen by the equation model (literal number / constant-only expression in the equation), not things that merely inherit “strength 3”.

Copilot Chat copilot/gpt-5.2 thought for 27s

Yes. Based on what we’ve now actually run, the Gemini solver’s failures are not “random” — they follow from a few specific design choices.

1) It only solves over the variables you pass in (initialVars)

  • In it sets varNames = Object.keys(initialVars) and then compiles every expression as new Function(...varNames, ...).
  • Any symbol that appears in an equation but isn’t in initialVars is effectively treated as “not a variable” (it won’t be substituted). Depending on the expression it either throws during compilation (then becomes () => NaN) or evaluates to ReferenceError (caught → NaN in solved helper).
  • This is a big semantic mismatch with “equations define the variable universe”. It also means “works when pasted in console” often depends on you having included *every* variable key up front (including intermediates like v1).

2) It does gradient descent on “pairwise differences”, not equation residuals, and it can converge to wrong local minima

  • It computes totalError as the sum of squared diffs between adjacent terms in each equation list:
  • For ['2x+3y', 33] it minimizes $(2x+3y - 33)^2$.
  • For ['5x-4y', 2] it minimizes $(5x-4y - 2)^2$.
  • That sounds fine, but the implementation’s update step is a *finite-difference gradient estimate* with a moving RMS cache and clipped step size. With the current hyperparameters, it’s simply not converging to the true solution for the simultaneous system; it gets stuck around (x≈4.34, y≈3.58).
  • This isn’t a JS/Node vs browser issue — we got the same wrong point in Puppeteer/Chromium.

3) It “fills NaNs with 0.5” (silent defaults), which changes the problem

  • After its propagation pass, it does for(...) if(isNaN(values[i])) values[i] = 0.5;.
  • That means unknowns are not “unknown”; they become a specific numeric guess and then get optimized from there. This can bias outcomes and hide the fact that it never derived a variable.
  • It also clashes with the “fail loudly” philosophy you stated earlier.

4) Its “pinning” semantics are not the same as Reciplier’s

  • It marks a variable as “pinned” (hard) when it is set from an anchor with anchorH===3 (literal / no-deps), and then it refuses to change it during gradient descent.
  • That’s a solver-internal concept, not the same thing as “user-frozen” vs “temporarily frozen while typing”. In Reciplier, “frozen” is a UI/user concept, not an emergent property of how the solver happened to derive a value.

5) It does not handle underconstrained systems the way Reciplier expects (cheesepan failure)

  • The qual it fails (cheesepan r1 with x not frozen) is specifically about choosing a reasonable solution when there are multiple degrees of freedom.
  • Gemini’s solver drifts x toward ~0 and sends r,d,A off, because the optimization is free to move whichever variables aren’t pinned, and there’s no concept like “prefer to keep seeded values stable unless forced”.
  • Reciplier’s solver is much more “propagate from stable anchors and preserve guesses”; Gemini’s is more “optimize everything unless pinned”.

6) It uses heuristic dependency locking (dependencies) that can prevent needed adjustments

  • It registers “definitions” like a = 3x as dependencies and then enforces them during optimization.
  • That’s helpful for some cases, but it can also over-constrain the search space in ways that block solving the “real” constraints, depending on which direction it decides the dependency goes.

If you want to go deeper, I can walk through *one* failing case line-by-line (simultaneous equations or cheesepan) and point to the exact step where it makes an irreversible choice (NaN seeding, pinning, dependency registration, or gradient step). Which one do you want to focus on first?

Added the qual and found a real bug + an easy fix.

What I added

  • At the end of , I appended this qual:
  • check('Simultaneous equations', solvem([['2x+3y', 33], ['5x-4y', 2]], {x: 6, y: 0}), {x: 6, y: 7});

What Gemini was doing wrong (root cause)

  • In Gemini’s gradient descent, it computed totalError once per iteration, then updated values[i] in-place for each variable i.
  • For i>0, it was still using the *old* totalError from before earlier variables were updated, so the finite-difference gradient estimate was wrong (stale baseline). That’s why it got stuck at a bad point for coupled systems like the simultaneous equations.

Easy fix applied

  • I refactored the gradient descent to compute a fresh baseError for the current values inside the per-variable loop, and then compute grad = (errorPlus - baseError) / DELTA.
  • After that change, the new qual passes:
  • Gemini now returns approximately {x: 6.0059, y: 7.0066} for the simultaneous system, which is within the existing diff < 1e-1 tolerance used by the qual harness in .

Current status

  • npm run quals still passes (main app unchanged by this Gemini-only qual).
  • node quals/solver_quals.js shows Gemini is now correct on simultaneous equations, but it still fails the cheesepan “x not frozen” case and is barely off on pyzza: C=50 (the cross-runner’s tolerance there is tighter than Gemini’s own 1e-1).

That symptom makes sense, and yes — it was very likely caused by null being treated as 0 during expression eval.

Root cause

  • In JS arithmetic, null coerces to 0 (e.g. 3*null === 0).
  • On blur, sometimes seeds a cell’s value as null (to mean “unknown”). With the previous vareval() behavior, that made expressions like 3*x evaluate to 0, and the solver could cascade everything to zero even though you didn’t type anything.

Fix

  • Changed vareval() in so null/undefined variables are assigned NaN instead of null when building the evaluation scope. That makes “unknown” behave like unknown (propagates NaN) rather than silently becoming zero.

Verification

  • npm run quals passes after the change.
  • Quick sanity check: vareval('3*x', {x: null}) now returns NaN (not 0).

If you reload Pyzza and repeat “click x then click a”, it should no longer zero everything out. If it still does, tell me which exact fields change (and whether any were blank/invalid), and I’ll reproduce it via a targeted Puppeteer qual.

A few things to make explicit in that spec so it’s unambiguous (and keeps the solver/UI contract tight):

  • What “the cval of an equation” means numerically. After solvem returns assignments for variables, you still need a rule to compute each equation’s displayed cval from its expressions. E.g. “evaluate all expressions; pick the first finite value” vs “pick the most ‘trustworthy’ one” vs “average them.” Without this, two equivalent implementations can disagree on what to show.
  • Edited vs. unfrozen vs. frozen. You probably want three states:
  • *Frozen*: append the literal number to that equation.
  • *Unfrozen*: do not append a number.
  • *Actively being edited*: treat like frozen temporarily (append the current numeric parse if valid) so the user’s in-progress edit constrains the system; otherwise you’ll get jumpy UI. This is basically the “currently-edited cell counts as constrained” rule you already had.
  • Underconstrained systems policy (fail vs. pick a convention). If there are zero frozen equations (or not enough constraints), solvem can’t determine a unique solution (scale/translation degrees of freedom). You need to decide one of:
  • “Fail loudly / show indeterminate,” or
  • “Choose a convention” (e.g., pick target 1 for a totally targetless equation) to get a deterministic solution.

This matters for examples like {a = 2b} with nothing frozen: there are infinitely many solutions.

  • Symbol discovery / missing-vars behavior. Today the solver contract has been “fail loudly if any symbol appears in equations but is not present in the initial vars object.” If you “drop cvars,” you still need a clear rule for constructing the initial vars map:
  • likely: “collect all symbols from all expressions; initialize them from previous solve results (or null)”.

Also specify what happens with unknowns (we’ve been treating null/undefined as NaN in evaluation to avoid null → 0 coercion).

  • Brace parsing edge cases. If the entire template is “text with {…} equation blocks,” define:
  • whether braces can be escaped / literal braces in text,
  • whether nested braces are allowed (probably “no”),
  • whitespace/newline rules,
  • what constitutes an “equation” inside braces (single = only? allow chaining like a=b=c?).
  • Validation/error model. Decide what happens when:
  • an expression can’t be parsed/preprocessed,
  • evaluation throws (domain errors, sqrt(-1)),
  • the system is inconsistent (no solution),
  • the user input is not a valid number (keep raw text + mark invalid + don’t constrain).

You don’t need fancy recovery, but the spec should say “don’t silently coerce” and “surface invalid/inconsistent.”

  • “They should all yield the same value” needs a tolerance rule. Pure === will make fields flicker red from float noise. Something like: compare with tolerance $|a-b| \le \epsilon\cdot \max(1,|a|)$.

The gotcha is no-op focus: focusing a field whose current cval is solver-derived will temporarily constrain the system to that derived value. That can be surprising if you tab around without typing: you’re freezing/unfreezing values moment-to-moment.
The minimal crisp rule I’d write is:

  • The cell object has only fix (frozen) plus the current raw input string.
  • When building solver equations: append the numeric literal iff (fix is true) OR (this cell is the active input AND its raw string parses to a finite number).

That implies two unavoidable ifs:

  • if (parsed is finite) append literal else don’t (and mark invalid)
  • if (eqn expressions don’t match within tolerance) mark red

  1. Symbol discovery: yes, same as status quo, but specify what counts as a symbol (ident regex) and what gets excluded (reserved words like sqrt, sin, etc).

  • If you want cute/short and “parse-y”: varse(expr) works, but I’d explicitly define it in the spec once (“varse = extract variable symbols”).
  • If you want less opaque: vextract(expr) or varsOf(expr) is clearer.
  • A compromise I like: varsIn(expr) (reads well, not too long).

One more thing you didn’t mention that’s worth pinning down: display formatting vs stored numeric value. If you freeze using the rounded display string, you’re pinning the rounded number (e.g. 6.28), not the underlying float. The spec should say cval is numeric, formatting is separate, and freezing uses the numeric cval (or explicitly uses the displayed rounded value if that’s the intention).

Here’s the core tension with the dial recipe, and how I’d reason about what the quals *should* assert.

1) What “dial” is mathematically
It’s essentially:

  • Inputs you intend to specify: y0,m0,d0,vini and y,m,d,vfin
  • Derived intermediates: tini = unixtime(...), tfin = unixtime(...)
  • Derived output: r = (vfin - vini) / (tfin - tini)
  • Presentation: r*SID, r*SIW, r*SIM

So the one hard requirement for “works at all” is:
\[
tfin - tini \ne 0
\]
Otherwise r is undefined / infinite.

2) Why your current dial state trips “errors”
Right now your template has start date = end date (at least in the version I saw in the repo). With hidden constraints enabled, that implies tfin === tini, so (vfin-vini)/(tfin-tini) becomes division-by-zero → Infinity/NaN/non-finite, and the app’s “initial contradiction” checker flags that.

That’s not a “unixtime not available” problem; it’s a “the constraints imply a non-finite value” problem.

3) Decide what the *intended UX contract* is
This is the key decision for what quals should do. Two plausible specs:

A) Dial must load “clean” (no errors)

  • Then the dial template must not imply division-by-zero on load.
  • Without changing the template, the only way to achieve “clean on load” would be changing program behavior (e.g., skipping contradiction checks for some cases, or treating division-by-zero as “unknown” instead of error), which conflicts with your “fail loudly” / anti-Postel vibe.

B) Dial is allowed to load “loudly wrong” until you change an input

  • Then it’s *correct* for dial to show an error on load if tfin==tini.
  • The qual should assert the specific loud failure mode, and also assert that a minimal edit (e.g., change end day) clears the error and yields a finite r.

Given the general design principles you’ve written down (fail loudly; don’t silently paper over), B feels more consistent unless you explicitly want dial to be “drop-down safe”.

4) What I think the dial quals should assert (assuming option B)
I’d make dial have its own dedicated qual (not included in the “every recipe loads sanely” loop) that checks:

  • unixtime(...) evaluates (so no “undefined variable unixtime” errors).
  • On initial load: there is an error, and it’s specifically a contradiction / non-finite derived-rate situation (not undefined vars).
  • After changing *one* input to make tfin > tini (e.g., increment end date by 1 day): errors clear and r becomes finite; optionally also check (tfin-tini)/SID equals the displayed “days later” value if you have that exposed.

If instead you want option A (“dial must load clean”), then the qual is simple (no errors on load) — but that implies the template needs distinct default dates (or some other way to avoid tfin==tini).

That contradiction was real, and it was a solvemAss stability/propagation bug (not a unixtime bug).

What was happening

  • In dial, y0/m0/d0/y/m/d/vini/vfin are “singleton” vars (they come from cells like {vfin = 100100} which become singleton equations like ['vfin'] plus seeded initial values).
  • tini/tfin are then computed from those via equations like ['tini', 'unixtime(y0,m0,d0)'].
  • But solvemAss was treating “just-solved this pass” vars as *not stable* whenever there exists any constrained variable in the system (here SID is constrained by ['SID', 86400]), so tini/tfin weren’t considered stable inputs for the later equation r = (vfin-vini)/(tfin-tini).
  • Result: tini/tfin could be right, the RHS could be $1.1586$, but r stayed at its seed value 1, triggering the contradiction banner.

Fix

  • Updated solvemAss in to track a new per-pass set solvedFromStableThisPass.
  • isStable(v) now checks solvedFromStableThisPass (instead of the old constrained.size === 0 && solvedThisPass.has(v) gating).
  • Added a few new if checks of the form if (isTrustworthy || targetIsStable) ... to mark variables as stable-within-pass when they were solved from a trustworthy/stable target.

The difference isn’t “this recipe vs other recipes”; it’s “a bare number acting as a *seed value* vs acting as an *actual constraint*”, and right now the code only treats the number as a constraint in one specific shape.

What the code currently treats as a constraint

In the initial solve, the solver only sees a numeric constraint for a cell if buildEquations decides to append the cell’s cval to the equation list. And it only does that when cell.fix is true:

  • parseCell sets cell.fix to “the *first* =-part is a constant”.
  • buildEquations in does: if (cell.fix && cell.cval !== null) eqn.push(cell.cval).

So:

  • {33 = 2x + 3y} → first part is numeric → fix=true → solver gets ['2x+3y', 33] (a real constraint).
  • {b1*60 = 26} → first part is not numeric → fix=false → solver gets only ['b1*60'] (no constraint).

Why {x = 7} “gets respected” elsewhere

With {x = 7}, the 7 is not being enforced as an equation unless it’s written with the number first ({7 = x}).

What *does* happen is:

  • buildInitialValues seeds x = 7 when it sees a single-variable cell with a numeric cval.
  • If nothing else forces x to move, the solver leaves it at 7, so it *looks* “respected”.

In biketour, b1 is used downstream (b = b1+b2+b3, t = w-b, etc). Since {b1*60 = 26} never becomes a constraint, b1 remains just a seed/guess and can get moved around by the rest of the system.

Is the spec wrong? What’s the “right” solution?

Given how equations normally work, the principled fix is: treat {expr = number} and {number = expr} symmetrically as constraints (i.e., the presence of exactly one bare number in a multi-part cell should yield an equation containing that number, regardless of which side it’s on).

That would make {b1*60 = 26} actually constrain b1 to 26/60 during the initial solve, and it would also make {x = 1} truly pinned (which seems aligned with the “bare numbers start frozen” intent you referenced).

Your proposal is coherent, and (importantly) it reuses an existing distinction we already have instead of redefining what = means.

Conceptually, what you’re describing is a constraint-priority / constraint-relaxation scheme:

  • Treat every numeric literal in a cell as a constraint candidate (so {b1*60 = 26} actually constrains something).
  • But don’t *commit* to all of them being hard constraints: if they overconstrain the system, relax some.

That’s strictly “less drastic” than changing the semantics of = itself (eg making {x = 7} always mean “pin x”), but it *is* still a global behavioral shift: numbers stop being “just seeds” and become “soft pins”.

The good part

  • It fixes the biketour symptom naturally: b1*60=26 starts life as a real constraint, so you get b1=26/60 immediately, unless it conflicts with something else.
  • It doesn’t require any new syntactic rule like “numbers must be on the left”.

The tricky parts (where it can go off the rails)

  1. Non-determinism / order dependence

“Remove constants one at a time until sat” is a greedy algorithm. If you don’t specify the removal order, you’ll get surprising outcomes depending on iteration order.

  1. Anti-Postel / fail-loudly tension

If we silently drop constraints, the app “succeeds” but the user doesn’t know which literals were ignored. That’s the classic footgun. The scheme can still be aligned with fail-loudly *if* we surface which constants got relaxed (eg via the banner / invalid highlights), but that’s UX work.

  1. What is ‘hard’ vs ‘soft’?

The cleanest way to avoid ad-hoc branching is to use the categories you already have:

  • user-frozen cells (state.fixedCellIds) are hard constraints
  • everything else with a numeric literal is soft
  • (optionally) the current edit cell’s literal is hard *during edit* (already true)

Then the relaxation loop only ever removes soft literals, never hard ones. That’s a principled hierarchy, not “if this recipe then that”.

What I’d recommend if we implement it

  • Make the initial attempt “maximally constrained” *only by adding soft literals*, keeping user-frozen literals hard.
  • If unsat, relax soft literals in a deterministic priority order (eg: relax literals from cells that are not single-variable identifiers first; or relax the ones that participate in the largest violated residual; etc — but we’d pick one and lock it down with quals).
  • And crucially: record which literals were relaxed so it’s auditable (even if we only expose it in debug at first).

Because in the current UI parser, a variable is only “defined” if it appears as a standalone identifier expression inside a cell.

Concretely:

  • buildSymbolTable treats something as a definition only when a cell’s ceqn contains an expression matching /^[a-zA-Z_][a-zA-Z0-9_]*$/ (like x, b1, tau, etc).
  • Your cells:
  • {1x} parses as an expression 1x (references x, but does not *define* x)
  • {x/2 = 2} parses into ceqn = ['x/2'] plus a numeric cval = 2 (again references x, but does not contain the standalone identifier x)
  • So symbols never gets x, and then the reference-scanning pass sees x in 1x / x/2 and reports “undefined variable x”.

This is why recipes typically include something like {x = 1} or {x} somewhere: it creates the explicit definition entry for x in the symbol table.

Separately (related to the earlier b1*60=26 issue): even after you define x, {x/2 = 2} still won’t currently act as a numeric constraint unless the number is on the left (or you change the constraint handling), because the initial solver only treats certain bare numbers as constraints.

What’s actually ambiguous / “buggy” in the spec right now is: what does it mean for a symbol to be “defined”?

  • If “defined” means “appears in a standalone {x} or {x = ...} cell”, then {x/2 = 8} *should* be an error unless you also add {x} somewhere.
  • If “defined” means “appears anywhere in any cell”, then the whole notion of “undefined variable” goes away, and {b = a+z} would quietly introduce z (which is anti‑Postel because typos become silent new variables).

So we need to choose, explicitly, which world we want.

Two coherent designs (pick one)

  1. Black-box equations (no undefined-variable errors)
  • Every identifier that appears anywhere is a variable.
  • All cells are just equations/expressions; solver tries to satisfy them all; if inconsistent, you get contradictions.
  • Pro: {x/2 = 8} “just works” with no special cases, and a bunch of current symbol-table logic can be deleted.
  • Con: typos become new variables; you lose loud failures for misspellings unless we add some other loudness mechanism.
  1. Declared-variable language (keep undefined-variable errors)
  • Variables must be declared explicitly (eg {x} or {x = 1} or some other explicit declaration form).
  • {x/2 = 8} without an {x} is *supposed* to error; the fix is to change templates, not the parser.
  • Pro: typo detection stays loud, consistent with anti‑Postel.
  • Con: templates are more verbose; less “nice black box”.

There’s also a hybrid (“constraints may introduce vars, but assignments don’t”) — that’s basically where the duct tape comes from; it’s hard to explain and makes the language feel magical.

That phrase is basically “soft constraints” / preferences. A pure equation solver doesn’t have “if possible”: constraints are either satisfiable together or not. That algorithm is internally consistent, but only under a very specific interpretation:

  • Constants in the template are used to (a) check the template is satisfiable at load time, and (b) provide initial/default values for what the UI fields start as.
  • After initialization, constants only continue to matter if the cell is frozen (either because it started with a constant, or the user toggled it).

If that’s what you want, then yes: steps 1–4 “work” together.

Where it bites (important edge cases)

  • {x = 1} becomes a default, not a constraint. After step 4, ceqn = ['x'], and unless frozen, there is no remaining “=1” constraint in the live system. That matches your parenthetical: you want a way to set defaults without fixing.
  • {6.28 = tau} starts frozen, so tau is constrained to 6.28 forever (until unfrozen). Again matches your convention.
  • {x/2 = 8} under this algorithm is also only a *default* unless frozen (because step 4 removes the 8 from ceqn). So after initialization, the system is free to move away from 8 without it even counting as a violated constraint. That’s the key point: in this model, writing = 8 does *not* mean “keep honoring 8”, it means “start at 8”.

So the question becomes: do you want {x/2 = 8} to behave like {x = 1} (a default), or like {6.28 = tau} (a hard constraint unless unfrozen)?

If you want “honor {x/2=8} if possible” *without freezing it*, that’s not represented by your step 4 model. “If possible” is a soft constraint / prioritization layer: when the user edits something else, you’d prefer to keep x/2 near 8, but you’re willing to violate it to satisfy higher-priority constraints. A plain satisfiability solver doesn’t express that without either:

  • adding constraint priorities/weights (optimization), or
  • keeping it as a hard constraint and letting the user explicitly unfreeze it when they’re ok with violating it.

Two crisp spec choices

  1. Defaults-only constants (your 4-step algorithm as written):
  • Any constant not in the first position is just an initial value that disappears after step 4.
  • {x/2=8} is merely a default.
  1. Constraints persist unless unfrozen:
  • Keep constants as part of the live constraint system (not removed in step 4), but treat “frozen” as “also pin the cell’s *field value*”.
  • Then {x/2=8} remains a constraint forever (unless you introduce a way to mark it “not a constraint”, i.e., defaults-vs-constraints syntax).

Given the rest of your README, the current language already uses position to disambiguate “hard constraint (starts frozen)” vs “default (not frozen)”. Under that, {x/2=8} is ambiguous: it looks like a constraint but behaves like a default in your algorithm.

If you want, I can help you formalize a single rule that resolves that ambiguity without adding new conditionals in code (i.e., by changing the template syntax/spec rather than heuristics).

What Fails (Concrete)

  • With biketour loaded and “Avg speed” edited to 15, the *only* equation that ends up failing is the edited one:
  • Equation: ['v', 'd/t', 15]
  • Evaluates to: [15, 12.6923076923, 15]
  • The default frozen cells at that moment are exactly:
  • 66 = d, 13 = H, 00 = M, 0 = b3
  • So the banner “Overconstrained!” is coming from “unsat + there exists a frozen cell”, but the deeper issue is: the solver never updates t (or anything upstream) to make d/t match the new v.

Why It Fails (Mechanism)
There are two separate solver limitations showing up here:

  1. Solving d/t = 15 for t fails because solveFor brackets across a discontinuity at 0.

When v is pinned to 15 and d is pinned to 66, the solver needs t = 66/15 = 4.4.
Internally, it tries to solve the expression d/t for t, but the current bracketing logic considers values at t = +scale and t = -scale and treats a sign-change as a root bracket. For d/t, that produces a false bracket around 0 (the function jumps from $-\infty$ to $+\infty$), so the binary search can’t converge to the real positive root and solveFor returns null. Result: t stays at its old value, so d/t stays 12.6923....

  1. When you “unfreeze all”, a different limitation prevents recomputing derived values.

In the unfreeze-all scenario, the first failing equation becomes:

  • ['u', 'd/w'] with values [10.56, 12.48]

This happens because in 2-term “definition-looking” equations like u = d/w, the solver currently tends to pick the *existing value of u* as the “target” when nothing is “trustworthy”, and then it refuses to adjust the other side unless the target is trustworthy/stable. So u doesn’t get updated to follow d/w after other variables shift.

Net-net

  • The biketour system *should* be solvable after changing v; the solver just fails to propagate the change through a division constraint and also fails to “refresh” definition variables like u in some cases.

If you want, I can implement a fix. It will likely involve:

  • Adjusting solveFor bracketing to avoid false brackets across discontinuities (this will require at least one new if to reject/avoid brackets crossing singularities like t=0), and/or
  • Teaching solvemAss to treat 2-element equations of the form [simpleVar, expr] directionally (so the simple var follows the expression even when nothing is “trustworthy”).

Copilot Chat copilot/gpt-5.2 thought for 1m46s

Yes, it can be correct for it to say “No solution” for many numbers you type into the dial “rate” fields — and it’s not primarily floating-point rounding, it’s discreteness.

  • In the dial template script.js, the end time is constrained by tfin = unixtime(y,m,d). With that, tfin is always exactly midnight UTC on some calendar day, so tfin - tini = n \cdot SID for some integer $n$ (whole days).
  • With vini=73 and vfin=70, the rate-per-day field is constrained to $r\cdot SID = (vfin-vini)/n = -3/n$. That means only values like -1 (n=3), -0.5 (n=6), -0.75 (n=4), etc are exactly satisfiable. Something like -0.8 would require $n=3.75$ days, which is impossible if y,m,d must be integers.
  • If you edit the per-second field (the one titled like r = (vfin-vini)/(tfin-tini)), typing -1 means $-1$ kg/sec (i.e., $-86400$ kg/day). That would imply tfin-tini=3 seconds, which also can’t be represented by unixtime(y,m,d) with day granularity. So you’ll get “No solution” very quickly there.
  • “Too close to zero” is a different failure mode: it implies an enormous duration $(tfin-tini)=\frac{-3}{r}$, which can push the date far away; eventually JS date ranges and/or solver numerics can break. But the common “No solution” you’re seeing is the integer-day constraint, not precision.

If you want “never show No solution while typing rates”, you need a spec change (and I’d implement it, but it’s a behavioral change):

  • Option A (least magic): add an explicit end time-of-day variable to the dial recipe so tfin can match arbitrary durations exactly (still fails loudly if dates go out of range).
  • Option B: treat the edited rate as a soft constraint: pick the nearest satisfiable end date and leave the rate field red (violated) instead of claiming unsat.

Say which option you prefer and I’ll do it (it will require at least one new if in the UI/solver path; I’ll call it out explicitly).

function updateInvalidExplainBannerInDom() {

  const rendered = document.querySelector('#recipeOutput .recipe-rendered')

  const txt = shouldShow

  el && (el.textContent = txt, el.hidden = !shouldShow)

The Simeq Bug Explained

What the test does:

  1. Load the simeq recipe: 2*{x = 6} + 3*{y} = {33 = 2x + 3y} and 5*{x} - 4*{y} = {2 = 5x - 4y}
  2. Find the unfrozen {x} cell (the one with title just "x", not "x = 6")
  3. Type "60" into that field
  4. Press Tab to blur

What's happening:

  1. User types "60" → during handleFieldInput, the solver tries to satisfy x=60 with {x = 6} frozen → fails → sets banner "No solution found"
  2. User presses Tab → during handleFieldBlur, the code does a fallback (solving without the edited constraint)
  3. The fallback succeeds (x=6, y=7 satisfies all constraints) → x value snaps back to "6" ✓

Why this is highest leverage

  • Equation evaluation logic is duplicated with slightly different tolerances and invariants across those functions, which is a reliability risk; a core module lets us centralize that once.
  • A pure core can be qual’d without DOM, giving you confidence for changes that touch the solver boundary.

Scope sketch

  • New file like recipcore.js exporting pure functions: checkBraceSyntax, extractCells, parseCell, buildSymbolTable, buildEquations, buildInitialEquations, buildInitialSeedValues, buildInteractiveEqns, recomputeCellCvals, isCellViolated, getUnsatisfiedCellIds, contradictionsForEqns.
  • Add a single orchestrator like solveRecipe({text, fixedCellIds, edit}) -> {cells, values, errors, invalidIds, banners}.
  • reciplier.js just calls that and renders; csolver.js remains unchanged.

Boundary definitions, in this codebase:

  • UI layer (reciplier.js): DOM, events, rendering, banners, input parsing/formatting. It should not know how equations are evaluated beyond calling a solver API.
  • “Core” (still in reciplier.js if you want): pure parsing/validation/eqn construction and orchestration. It takes text + edit state and returns {cells, eqns, seed, values, errors, invalidIds} without touching DOM or globals.
  • Solver (csolver.js): understands expressions, equations, variables, and assignments. It should not know about cells, urtext, frozen state, or UI. It already provides preval, vareval, varparse, isconstant, isbarevar, solvem.

Where the reciplier↔solver boundary is fuzzy today:

  • reciplier.js re‑implements equation satisfaction in contradictionsForEqns, getUnsatisfiedCellIds, and isCellViolated instead of using solvem’s zij/sat. That’s solver‑adjacent logic living in the UI layer.
  • checkInitialContradictions does a full evaluation pass over eqns with its own tolerance logic, again duplicating solver behavior.
  • logFailedSolve constructs solver diagnostics (Mathematica syntax) in the UI layer.

A clean boundary (without a new file) would look like:

  • Reciplier builds eqns and seed (core responsibility), calls solvem, and then uses solvem’s zij/sat to decide invalid cells and banners. This keeps equation satisfaction logic inside the solver’s canonical path.
  • Reciplier uses vareval/varparse only for parsing and UI display (allowed per README), not for determining global satisfiability.
  • Any solver diagnostics live next to the solver, or are driven by a solver return value (e.g., solvem could optionally include a debug payload), rather than UI formatting its own.

So: the “core vs UI” boundary is about side effects; the “reciplier vs solver” boundary is about who owns equation evaluation and satisfaction logic. Tightening the latter mostly means deleting or bypassing the duplicate evaluation paths in reciplier.js and relying on solvem’s zij/sat instead. That doesn’t require a new file, just consolidation.

21:10
here's how claude answered. which of you is correct?

The issue is the missing touch-action CSS property on the range inputs.

On mobile, when you touch and drag on a slider, the browser interprets horizontal movement as a scroll/pan gesture by default. The browser intercepts the touch before the slider can respond to it. Tapping works because that's a discrete event, not a continuous drag.

The fix is to add touch-action: none (or touch-action: pan-y if you want to allow vertical scrolling while dragging) to the range input styles in style.css:98-105:


input[type="range"] {
  /* existing styles... */
  touch-action: none;  /* prevents browser from hijacking touch for scrolling */
}
This tells the browser "don't handle touch gestures on this element - let the element handle them directly."

Codex gpt-5.2-codex (xhigh) thought for 20s

Event handling is UI‑specific, so it lives in reciplui.js. It should not import reciplier.js. Instead, reciplier.js is the composition root that wires dependencies:

  • reciplui.js exports initUI({ dispatch, render }) (or similar) and only calls dispatch(action) on user events.
  • recipengine.js (or recipstate.js) exports reduce(state, action) and returns the next state (pure, no DOM).
  • reciplier.js holds the current state, calls reduce on each action, then calls render(state) in the UI module.

So yes, UI events “call back,” but only via a callback that reciplier.js passes in. That avoids cyclic imports and keeps the UI ignorant of solver/parse details.

Why:

// reciplui.js
export function initUI(root, dispatch) {
  root.addEventListener('input', e => {
    const action = extractAction(e)
    if (action) dispatch(action)
  })
}

export function renderUI(state) {
  // DOM updates only
}

// reciplier.js
import { initUI, renderUI } from './reciplui.js'
import { reduce } from './recipengine.js'

let state = initialState()
initUI(document, action => {
  state = reduce(state, action)
  renderUI(state)
})

Option 2 is valid if you want reciplui.js to be a dumb renderer, but it pulls DOM/event code back into reciplier.js and blurs the UI/engine boundary.

Tradeoff lens:

  • Option 1 (UI owns events + dispatch): keeps DOM concerns inside reciplui.js, keeps state/solve pure, avoids cyclic imports, and makes the UI replaceable/testable. Cost is a callback, but it can be just one dispatch(action); no callback sprawl.
  • Option 2 (main owns events): fewer indirections in a tiny app, but reciplier.js becomes DOM‑heavy and harder to keep pure logic separate. It tends to accrete UI details over time.

If callbacks feel annoying, the usual fix is “one callback, many actions.” reciplui.js binds events, translates them into action objects, and calls dispatch(action). That’s a single dependency injection point, not a bunch of bespoke callbacks.

recipstate.js would hold the *pure* business logic: “given text + prior state + an edit, compute the next state.” No DOM. No event binding. No timers.

“State transitions” means functions like:
state' = applyEdit(state, {type: 'edit', cellId, value})
“Domain model” means the definitions of cell, state, solve, and the invariants derived from the spec (eg, how ceqn, cval, and fixedCellIds relate).

Most of the spec’s business logic (parsing rules, freezing rules, colon init rules, constraints, errors, solver use, banner logic) belongs in recipstate.js. The UI is just a view of the state.

With plain <script> tags, the split is mostly organizational: it improves navigation and diff hygiene but does not give encapsulation. Everything still lands on globalThis, and dependencies are order‑sensitive. That’s the core “smell.”

If you want explicit boundaries/exports, you need one of these:

  • Option 1: ES modules. Convert files to export/import, then load a single entry module via <script type="module" src="recipmain.js">. recipmain.js would import reciplui, reciplogic, etc., then call init(). This gives explicit dependencies and eliminates globals. It also requires updating Node quals to run in ESM (or a bundler), and updating the csolver.js CommonJS require path.
  • Option 2: Global namespace object (minimal change). Create a single namespace (e.g., globalThis.Recip) and have each file assign its exports there and consume from there. This keeps script tags, keeps Node quals simple, reduces global sprawl, and makes dependencies explicit without ESM. Still order‑sensitive, but much clearer.
  • Option 3: Bundler. Use esbuild/rollup to bundle ESM into one browser file. HTML loads one bundle. This is the cleanest runtime but adds a build step and tooling.

If your immediate concern is the one‑line reciplier.js, a small step is to move the DOMContentLoaded hookup into reciplui.js and drop reciplier.js. That doesn’t fix the global namespace issue, but it removes the “empty entrypoint” smell.

Which direction do you want to take? My recommendation if you want explicit boundaries without a tooling shift is Option 2 (namespace object). If you want real module encapsulation, Option 1 or 3 is the way.

You're right to push back. Let me think about this properly.

Best practice analysis:

The standard convention across most UIs is chevron on the LEFT:

  • macOS Finder disclosure triangles
  • VS Code file explorer and sidebar sections
  • HTML <details> element default styling
  • Bootstrap/Material accordions
  • Tree views in virtually every IDE

The reasoning: users expect the toggle affordance at the start of the row, following natural left-to-right scanning. Clicking at the beginning of a header to expand/collapse is deeply ingrained.

Chevron on the right is typically used for navigation (e.g., "go to this page" arrows in mobile lists), not expand/collapse.

I'll move the chevron to the left. Let me make that change:

I see the current implementation has <span class="debug-chevron">▼</span> at the start of the header text, but before the emoji. Let me look at how other well-designed UIs handle this.

The user is right — having the chevron on the left is standard. Currently it's technically on the left but embedded in the text flow. I'll make it cleaner by positioning it at the very start, separate from the text, and ensure the styling is clear.

Done. The chevron is now on the left, which is the standard convention:

  • Chevron positioned at the start of the header (left side) using flexbox with gap: 0.5rem
  • Made chevron slightly smaller (0.75rem) so it doesn't compete with the header text
  • Header still centered overall, but chevron leads visually

This follows the pattern used in macOS Finder, VS Code, and most accordion/tree-view UIs where the disclosure triangle is always on the left.

function solveByGaussian(eqns, vars, inf, sup) {

Option C follows anti-magic most literally — no if-statements! But it's wasteful. However, in the spirit of "the beauty of NP-complete problems is it's easy to check candidate solutions" (from the csolver.js comments), this might actually be the right approach.

The key insight: We don't need solvers to know whether they apply. We just need them to produce a candidate solution. The orchestrator checks if it's valid with eqnsSatisfied. If not, try the next solver.

This means:

  2. Every solver returns {ass, zij, sat} — never null
  3. The orchestrator just picks the first sat=true result

The "if-statement" becomes: does the candidate satisfy the constraints? That's not special-casing, it's just the definition of a solution.

This is a brilliant insight from the thinker! Let me share this with you:

The Anti-Magic Architecture: Composable Refinement Passes

Instead of asking "does this solver apply?" (which requires an if-statement), we treat every solver as a refinement pass that extracts what structure it can handle:

function solvem(eqns, vars, inf, sup) {
  let ass = { ...vars }
  
  // Phase 1: Gaussian on linear parts (always runs, might do nothing)
  ass = gaussianOnLinearParts(eqns, ass)
  
  // Phase 2: Propagation (always runs)
  ass = propagate(eqns, ass)
  
  // Phase 3: Bisection on stubborn equations (always runs)
  ass = bisectRemaining(eqns, ass)
  
  return { ass, zij: zidge(eqns, ass), sat: eqnsSatisfied(eqns, ass) }
}

Key insight: Every equation has a linear part and a nonlinear residual:

  • 3x + 2y = 7 → linear coefficients: [3, 2, 7], residual: 0
  • x^2 + y = 5 → linear coefficients: [0, 1, 5], residual: x²
  • x^2 + 2x = 3 → linear coefficients: [2, 0, 3], residual: x²

Gaussian elimination runs on the linear parts. If a row is all zeros (pure nonlinear), it does nothing for that equation. The nonlinear residuals get handled by propagation/bisection.

Zero "does this apply?" checks. The only decision point is the final eqnsSatisfied check — which is just the definition of success, not a special case.

This means:

  1. Solvers are sequential refinement passes, not mutually exclusive alternatives
  2. Each pass always runs and proposes refinements to the assignment
  3. The final satisfaction check is the only branching point

Does this architecture resonate with you? Before I start implementing, I want to make sure we're aligned on:

  1. Composable passes (Gaussian → Propagation → Bisection) vs. try-until-success (try Gaussian, if sat return, else try Propagation, etc.)
  1. How aggressive should Gaussian be? Should it only handle fully linear systems, or should it extract and solve the linear subsystem even from mixed systems?
  1. What to do with the current solvemPrimary's special cases (unixtime inversion, product scaling w*h)? Should they become their own refinement passes, or should we try to eliminate them entirely?

solvemPrimary's Special Cases Breakdown

1. Unixtime Inversion (~lines 460-510)

// Handle: tini = unixtime(y0, m0, d0)
// If we know tini (target), invert to find y0, m0, d0
const uargs = unixtimeArgs(expr)  // extracts {y, mo, d} variable names
if (uargs) {
  const inv = invertUnixtimeSeconds(target)  // convert seconds → {y, mo, d}
  // Set values[y], values[mo], values[d] from inv
}

Why it exists: unixtime(y,m,d) is not algebraically invertible — you can't solve for y,m,d from a timestamp using normal equation solving. It needs special date arithmetic.

2. Product Scaling (w*h) (~lines 515-560)

// Handle: when expression is exactly `a*b` (product of two variables)
// and we have a target value for the product
if (compact === `${a}*${b}` || compact === `${b}*${a}`) {
  // Scale both variables proportionally: newA = aVal * sqrt(target/current)
  const scale = Math.sqrt(target / current)
  newA = aVal * scale
  newB = bVal * scale
}

Why it exists: If you have w*h = 100 and need to change it to w*h = 200, there are infinitely many solutions. This heuristic scales both proportionally (preserving aspect ratio), which is useful for the "rectangular pan" use case in the spec.

3. Same-Variable-Both-Sides Equations (~lines 600-660)

// Handle: [['1/phi', 'phi - 1']]  (golden ratio)
// Both sides depend on the same single variable
// Create difference expression: (1/phi) - (phi - 1) = 0
// Then bisection search to find root

Why it exists: Normal propagation can't handle equations where the target and source both depend on the same variable. This special case detects that pattern and applies bisection.

Plan: Bring Codebase in Line with AGENTS.md Principles

Overview

The codebase has several areas that violate the Anti-Magic (minimize if-statements), Anti-Postel (fail loudly), and "Predict vs Verify" principles outlined in AGENTS.md. The most impactful improvements focus on the constraint solvers.

Key Violations to Address

1. Predict-vs-Verify Anti-patterns in Solvers (High Priority)

  • gaussJordan hasUnknowns check (csolver.js ~line 410): Predicts "if there are unknowns, bail early" instead of just trying and checking if the result satisfies the equations.
  • newtRaphson potentiallyUnderdetermined check (csolver.js ~line 1199): Same pattern - predicting failure rather than attempting and verifying.
  • newtRaphson zero-value bailout (csolver.js ~line 1271): Predicts Newton won't work with zeros instead of trying.

Fix: Let each solver attempt to find a solution unconditionally, then check sat. The solvem loop already handles fallback to the next solver.

2. Anti-Postel Violations (Silent Fallbacks)

  • Many return null patterns in solveFor that silently give up
  • toNum returns null on non-string input instead of throwing
  • Various places where invalid inputs are silently "handled" instead of crashing

Fix: Replace silent fallbacks with asserts/throws where the contract is violated.

3. If-Statement Heavy Code That Could Be Simplified

  • reciplui.js attachPegTrigger: Long chain of if (TRIGGER_MODES.has(...)) could be data-driven
  • reciplogic.js symtab: Series of if (cell.colonError === ...) checks
  • kludgeOrama: Self-described "abomination" with heavy conditional logic

4. Missing Quals

  • The README mentions a bug where clearing a field throws an error instead of being caught by quals
  • Need more quals covering edge cases like empty fields, undefined variables, etc.

Relevant Files

  • csolver.js - Primary target for predict-vs-verify fixes
  • reciplogic.js - Anti-Postel fixes and if-statement reduction
  • reciplui.js - Data-driven trigger mode handling
  • matheval.js - Input validation
  • quals/solver_quals.js - Add more edge-case quals

Notes

  • Changes should be discussed before implementing since adding/removing if-statements is a sensitive topic per AGENTS.md
  • The gaussJordan fix mentioned in AGENTS.md scratchpad is a good model: compute values and check if they work, rather than predicting failure
  • Per rule 8: "Fastidiously mention every if-statement you think you need, to me, the human"

Plan: AGENTS.md Principles Compliance

Overview

Apply Anti-Postel, Anti-Magic, and code quality principles across the remaining unchecked items in the AGENTS.md scratchpad. Focus on failing loudly, reducing unnecessary conditionals, and making dispatch logic data-driven.

Requirements

1. toNum Anti-Postel Fix (reciplogic.js)

  • Change if (typeof x !== 'string') return null to throw an error
  • Rationale: All callers pass input.value (always a string). A non-string is a programming bug that should crash, not silently return null
  • Keep returning null for empty string (valid user input when clearing a field)

2. Data-Driven Trigger Modes (reciplui.js)

  • Refactor attachPegTrigger from if-chain to dispatch table pattern
  • Create TRIGGER_HANDLERS object mapping mode names to handler functions
  • Iterate over TRIGGER_MODES and call corresponding handlers
  • Reduces ~50 lines to ~20, makes adding new trigger modes trivial

3. symtab Error Generation (reciplogic.js)

  • Refactor the series of if (cell.colonError === ...) checks to a lookup table
  • Create COLON_ERROR_MESSAGES map from error codes to message templates
  • Minor DRY improvement, can be done opportunistically

4. Anti-Postel Audit - Add Asserts

  • Search for other return null patterns that silently accept invalid inputs
  • Add explicit invariant checks (if (!condition) throw) where contracts are violated
  • Focus on function entry points where callers should never pass invalid data

5. Additional Quals

  • Add quals for edge cases like empty fields, undefined variables
  • Add quals that would catch the toNum contract violation (passing non-string)
  • Ensure coverage of the Anti-Postel changes

Notes

  • solvem seeding logic: Leave as-is. The complexity handles two distinct modes (initial load vs interactive update) with genuinely different requirements. The existing Anti-Robustness throws for missing vars are correct.
  • vareval error handling: Leave as-is. The {value, error} return pattern is a proper Result type, not Anti-Postel violation.
  • solveFor return null patterns: Leave as-is. "Couldn't solve" is a legitimate outcome, not an error.
  • Per AGENTS.md rule 8: All if-statements being added/modified will be explicitly mentioned for human review.

Relevant Files

  • reciplogic.js - toNum fix, symtab error table
  • reciplui.js - trigger mode dispatch table
  • quals/util_quals.js - add toNum contract violation quals
  • csolver.js - potential assert audit targets
  • matheval.js - potential assert audit targets
